description:
🚀Hey! We are Gravity Defiers, a team passionate about space, science, and technology. For NASA Space Apps Challenge, we're working on developing health-monitoring software for astronauts. We're looking for curious, creative, and enthusiastic people who love solving problems and building new things together.

Skills needed: Hardware, software, coding, web development, data analysis, AI/ML, and disaster response.

Let's innovate, collaborate, and think beyond Earth! 🌌
summary:
Astronauts on long missions have to watch their own health. Nobody on Earth can help them quickly, and they may not know what a bad reading means.

EVA-SUIT is a small wearable kit and a website that helps with that. We built it with an ESP32 board and sensors. They track heartbeat, muscle movement, breathing, brain activity, and the temperature and humidity inside the helmet. The readings go live to a 3D astronaut on the screen, built from NASA’s own model. The astronaut can click on any body part to see how it is doing.
When something looks wrong, the screen flashes red. We compare each reading to the limits NASA’s Human Research Program gives for spaceflight. Then the app gives a short checklist and walks the person through it, one step at a time. There is also an AI chat that knows their recent readings, so they can ask what is going on in plain words.
details:
EVA-SUIT is a wearable health monitor for astronauts, with a live website at gravitydefiers.pages.dev. The sensors sit in the suit and helmet, and an ESP32 board reads them and sends the data to the site over Bluetooth. Everything you see is real data, with nothing faked. The site shows a 3D astronaut built from NASA’s own model. You can click the helmet, chest, arms or legs, and a live screen opens for that part. You can also pull the suit apart in an “explode” view to look at each piece on its own.

The app tracks heart rate, ECG, breathing sound, muscle activity, motion, and the temperature and humidity inside the helmet. Electrodes read brain activity. An AI compares each reading with NASA’s limits and with the person’s own recent history. If something looks wrong, the screen flashes red, and an emergency checklist walks the astronaut through what to do, one step at a time. A chat assistant also sees the live readings, so the astronaut can just ask what is going on in plain words. One health score, based on NASA’s Standard Measures, shows how they are doing at a glance, and a button exports a medical report for the flight surgeons.

This matters because on a trip to the Moon or Mars, help from Earth is slow. The astronaut becomes the first doctor. EVA-SUIT helps them catch problems early and know what to do next, which fits NASA’s own worry about distance from Earth.

For the build, we used an ESP32, an MPU6050 for motion, an INMP441 microphone for breathing, a DHT11 for temperature and humidity, a heartbeat sensor, and ECG electrodes. The website uses Three.js for the 3D model, plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, Web Bluetooth for the connection, and an LLM API for the chat and analysis. We think the creative part is putting real hardware, a 3D body you can click, and an AI guide in one place. The screens also change with the mission phase, such as docked, transit, spacewalk, launch and landing.

We kept in mind that astronauts are busy and stressed, so the screens are simple and the checklists are short. We also tied everything back to NASA’s research on spaceflight hazards and risks, like heart changes, poor sleep, immune changes and mental strain.
